prompt: What does `-E` do to `npm install`?

choices.text: Installs the packages globally, for every project on the computer
choices.why: That is `-g`, which this course never uses.

choices.text: Skips the lockfile so installs are faster
choices.why: The lockfile is still written, and it should be committed.

choices.text: Writes exact versions
choices.why: Right: `58.0.21` rather than `~58.0.21`.

choices.text: Installs only the packages Expo approves of
choices.why: npm knows nothing about Expo; `npx expo install` is the one that looks up versions.

prompt: Why does `src/planner.ts` contain no component and no `View`?

choices.text: Rules without a screen are tested and reused without one
choices.why: Right: the test checks them in Node, and lesson 4 uses them unchanged.

choices.text: Metro refuses components outside `App.tsx`
choices.why: Components live in any file.

choices.text: TypeScript files cannot contain JSX
choices.why: A `.tsx` file can; this one has no reason to.

choices.text: So that it runs on the main thread, where the screen is drawn
choices.why: All of your JavaScript runs on the JavaScript thread.

prompt: With this course's data, how many minutes are planned in the week of Monday 19 October 2026?
npm reports advisories in packages Expo's tools depend on. Why not run `npm audit fix --force`?

choices.text: It needs a working internet connection to reach the registry
choices.why: So does every install; that is not the danger.

choices.text: Advisories are never real
choices.why: They are real; the question is whether the fix is worse.

choices.text: It deletes `package-lock.json` and every lockfile beside it
choices.why: It rewrites it, which is the problem.

choices.text: It would install `expo@51.0.39`, a different SDK
choices.why: Right: a forced fix ignores the pins that keep the project on SDK 58.

prompt: Put Metro's three steps in order.
items: serialise the modules into one bundle

prompt: You installed a package while `npx expo start` was running, and the app still says *Unable to resolve module*. What do you try first?

choices.text: Reinstall Node.js
choices.why: Node.js is fine; Metro's cache is stale.

choices.text: Restart the server with `--clear`
choices.why: Right: that empties Metro's cache.

choices.text: Delete `package-lock.json` and every `node_modules`, then install again from scratch
choices.why: Heavy, and it loses the exact versions; the cache is the likelier cause.

choices.text: Rename the package in `package.json`
choices.why: That breaks the install instead of fixing the cache.

prompt: When a development build starts on a phone, where does its JavaScript come from?

choices.text: A bundle compiled into the APK when it was built
choices.why: That is a release build; a debug APK carries none.

choices.text: The development server, which bundles it on request
choices.why: Right, like the `curl` in the capture.

choices.text: Expo's servers, once you have signed in to your account
choices.why: No account is involved in development.

choices.text: The Play Store
choices.why: The store never serves a development build.

prompt: You edit a component that holds a half-typed form, and the form keeps its text. You edit `src/planner.ts`, and the form empties. Why?

choices.text: `src/planner.ts` is cached forever and needs `--clear`
choices.why: It was picked up; that is why the app reloaded.

choices.text: Only `App.tsx` keeps state between edits
choices.why: Any component file does.

choices.text: The form had a bug that the reload fixed
choices.why: The form did nothing wrong.

choices.text: It exports functions rather than components, so Fast Refresh falls back to a full reload
choices.why: Right: state survives an edit to components, not to other modules.

prompt: `look.mjs` printed `heading "Study planner"`. Without `role="heading"` on that `<Text>`, what would a screen-reader user lose?

choices.text: Finding the screen's title by moving between headings
choices.why: Right: it would be one more line of text.

choices.text: The ability to tap the title and jump to the top of the screen
choices.why: A heading is not something to tap.

choices.text: Nothing, since the text is still read aloud
choices.why: Read, yes; found by heading, no.

choices.text: The planner's data
choices.why: The data is unchanged.

prompt: What does the web build NOT tell you about the planner?

choices.text: Whether the week's total is computed correctly
choices.why: That logic is the same JavaScript; the web build shows it.

choices.text: Which elements have a role
choices.why: The accessibility tree shows exactly that.

choices.text: How the native views look on a phone
choices.why: Right: a browser draws HTML in their place.

choices.text: Whether the app starts at all when the page loads
choices.why: It shows that too.

prompt: Why does the App test call `jest.useFakeTimers({ now: … })` before rendering?

choices.text: So the week is the course's, whatever day the test runs
choices.why: Right: otherwise `today()` reads the real clock and the total changes.

choices.text: To make the test run faster by skipping every real timer
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Jest refuses to render without fake timers
choices.why: It renders either way.

choices.text: To stop React re-rendering
choices.why: Timers do not control rendering.

prompt: To use `jest-expo`, `package.json` names it as Jest's ___.
A colleague suggests replacing the App test with a screenshot compared by eye. What does the test check that the screenshot cannot?

choices.text: The colours of the screen
choices.why: A screenshot shows colours; the test does not.

choices.text: How fast the app opens on a phone, measured against last week's build
choices.why: Neither measures that.

choices.text: That the heading is announced as one, and the total is computed
choices.why: Right: a picture of `75 of 125` looks the same hard-coded.

choices.text: Nothing; they are equivalent checks
choices.why: They check different things.

prompt: Which Java version does React Native 0.88's Gradle plugin ask for?

choices.text: Java 8
choices.why: Far too old for current Android builds.

choices.text: Java 17
choices.why: Right: `openjdk-17-jdk-headless` on Ubuntu.

choices.text: Java 11
choices.why: Not the one it asks for.

choices.text: Java 21
choices.why: Installed alone, the build stopped asking for a Java 17 toolchain.

prompt: `unzip -l` found no `index.android.bundle` in the debug APK. Why is that correct?

choices.text: The bundle failed to build and Gradle ignored the error
choices.why: Nothing failed; a debug build skips bundling on purpose.

choices.text: Android forbids JavaScript files in packages
choices.why: A release APK carries one.

choices.text: The bundle is inside `libhermes.so`
choices.why: That is the engine, not your code.

choices.text: A debug build fetches its JavaScript from the development server
choices.why: Right; a release build carries the bundle, as lesson 20 shows.

prompt: Match each value in the APK with where it came from.
Which of these runs the iOS simulator?

choices.text: A Windows computer with WSL 2
choices.why: Xcode does not run there.

choices.text: An Ubuntu virtual machine on a fast PC
choices.why: Speed is not the obstacle; Xcode needs macOS.

choices.text: A Mac with Xcode
choices.why: Right, and no developer account is needed for it.

choices.text: Expo Go on an Android phone
choices.why: That runs Android.

prompt: A phone and a laptop on a hotel's Wi-Fi cannot see each other. What does `npx expo start --tunnel` change, and at what cost?

choices.text: A public relay carries it: slower, and a third party sees it
choices.why: Right; worth knowing before using it on private code.

choices.text: It switches the phone to Bluetooth, which drains the battery
choices.why: No Bluetooth is involved.

choices.text: It compiles a development build in Expo's cloud, for a monthly fee
choices.why: That is EAS Build, a different thing.

choices.text: Nothing: hotel networks always allow it
choices.why: Those networks are exactly the ones that keep devices apart.

prompt: You build for an Android emulator on an Intel laptop. Which architecture flag fits, and why?

choices.text: `arm64-v8a`, because every Android device is ARM
choices.why: An emulator image for an Intel computer is x86_64.

choices.text: `armeabi-v7a`, the smallest
choices.why: Size does not choose an architecture.

choices.text: None: leave it off to build only what the emulator needs
choices.why: Leaving it off builds all four families, slowly.

choices.text: `x86_64`, matching the emulator's processor
choices.why: Right: the image that runs at near native speed there.

prompt: Which of these run with no phone, no emulator and no Mac? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `npm test`
choices.why: Yes: Jest runs in Node.

choices.text: the web build read by `look.mjs`
choices.why: Yes: Chromium on the computer.

choices.text: `./gradlew assembleDebug`
choices.why: Yes: it builds the APK; installing it is another matter.

choices.text: `npx expo run:ios`
choices.why: That needs Xcode, so a Mac.
